newsitem.title: USA: Boeing to force quick merger decision in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Boeing to force quick merger decision in U.S.

text.p: Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. said Wednesday they will swiftly file millions of documents with antitrust officials, insuring the United States acts before Europe on their $13.7 billion merger.

At the same time, McDonnell Douglas Chief Executive Officer Harry Stonecipher charged that the top European Union competition official, Karel Van Miert, was trying to trigger a "war," an accusation quickly denied in Brussels.
If they file soon, the American companies can force a U.S. government decision on their merger by mid-July, before the EU deadline at the end of that month.
The American companies say U.S. regulators are more objective and Stonecipher accused Van Miert of holding the merger "hostage."
"It's obvious he wants a war but I don't want a war," Stonecipher told reporters. In Brussels, Van Miert's spokesman quickly dismissed Stonecipher's comments as "totally nonsensical."
"Catastrophe or worst-case scenarios, we are not there," said Willy Helin, noting two months remain to negotiate.

Stonecipher's charges were the strongest yet, underscoring recent comments by American trade officials and senators from states with Boeing and McDonnell Douglas plants, who say they want the Europeans to be fair and impartial.
Some Americans say the Europeans are trying to protect their commercial airliner consortium, Airbus Industrie.

The American competition agency considering the Boeing merger, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), has remained silent as required by law. That suits Stonecipher fine, and the companies' actions insure that there will be an FTC decision soon.

American law sets stringent deadlines for the government to act on pending mergers. Once the FTC has all relevant documents -- Boeing alone will have 5 million pages -- it has 20 business days to act. That places the power over timing squarely in the hands of Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.
"The FTC will rule before the middle of July," Stonecipher confidently told reporters. He said that Boeing and McDonnell Douglas will deliver all documents to the FTC by mid-June at the latest.
Should the FTC discover problems with the merger, Stonecipher said, he is confident any necessary restructuring can take place quickly enough to keep the timing on track.
The FTC also has the authority to reject the transaction as anti-competitive.

A completed merger would create the world's largest aerospace company, producing military and space equipment, and cut the number of major commercial airplane manufacturers from three to two. But Stonecipher said his company's commercial airline business is fading.
"Douglas is not dead but dying," said Stonecipher. "It had only 3 percent to 4 percent of the commercial airline market last year," selling 38 planes.

Van Miert has expressed concern that the merger could be anticompetitive, leaving Airbus Industrie to compete with Boeing alone. He told Reuters last month the merger cannot be permitted as long as Boeing has exclusive 20-year contracts with Delta Airlines and AMR Corp.'s American Airlines.
"To hold the merger hostage for that is totally inappropriate," Stonecipher said. "He's influencing the stockmarket."
The European Union's competition authority operates in a manner somewhat different than that of the United States.
EU officials have said they expect to finish investigating the merger in 10 days or so and then will provide Boeing with a statement of any problems they find with the merger.

That will be followed by a closed hearing, with the final decision by the end of July. The EU cannot halt the merger, but can fine the merged company 10 percent of total annual worldwide gross income.
Boeing's stock rose 62.5 cents to $100.625, while McDonnell Douglas gained 62.5 cents to $59.75 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-afternoon.
